dv2_corporation_governance.topic: How the City of London Corporation is governed today

claims.text: The City of London Corporation's ward elections were held on 20 March 2025 for the 100 seats of the Court of Common Council; 51 seats make a majority.
In the 2025 election, 45 of the 100 councillors were returned unopposed, across 14 of the City's 25 wards.

Results in 2025: Independents 83 seats (up 5), Labour 7 (up 2), Temple & Farringdon Together 10 (unchanged), Castle Baynard Independents 0 (down 7). Ward-level turnout ranged from 11% (Farringdon Without) to 49% (Portsoken and Vintry).

Under the business franchise, a business may appoint one employee as a voter for every five staff, up to ten voters, and one additional voter for every fifty staff beyond that; residents each have one vote.
The Lord Mayor serves a one-year term, chairs both the Court of Aldermen and the Court of Common Council, and must already be an Alderman who has served as Sheriff.
Each of the 25 wards elects one Alderman for a six-year term; the Aldermen also sit in the Court of Common Council, alongside the 100 elected Common Councilmen.
Two Sheriffs serve one-year terms and are elected each Midsummer Day by the liverymen; the liverymen also meet in Common Hall each September to choose the Lord Mayor, usually by acclamation.
Common Council elections are traditionally not fought on party lines, and the Court has powers similar to those of a London borough council.
Travers (2013) put the City's residents at about 10,000 and the people working within its boundaries at about 300,000.

The office of Mayor was created in 1189; the Sheriffs were Crown appointments until 1199 and thereafter subordinate to the Mayor. Regular meetings of the common council began in 1376, and the Council has been elected since 1384.
Business votes are allocated on a sliding scale by workforce, and a 2003 franchise reform widened the business vote while giving more representation to residential wards.

No founding charter survives; the City is regarded as incorporated by prescription, can alter its own constitution by an Act of Common Council, and was not reformed by the Municipal Corporations Act 1835.
The Corporation carries out the functions of a London borough and is the police authority for the City, which has its own police force separate from the Metropolitan Police.
It supports the financial services industry and represents its interests, and was renamed the City of London Corporation in 2006 to distinguish it from the Greater London Authority.

In December 2012, after criticism of its financial transparency, the Corporation disclosed that City's Cash, its private endowment fund, held more than £1.3 billion; net assets were £2.3 billion as of March 2016.

The Corporation maintains about 10,000 acres of green space outside the Square Mile, including Hampstead Heath, Epping Forest and Burnham Beeches, and controls three independent schools and the Guildhall School of Music and Drama.
The Chairman of the Policy and Resources Committee is often described as the Corporation's de facto political leader; Chris Hayward has held the post since 5 May 2022.

The business vote, abolished in other British local elections in 1969, numbered about 24,000 in 2009, far exceeding resident voters; the City of London (Ward Elections) Act 2002 greatly increased the business franchise.
George Monbiot argued that the Corporation's power helps explain why bank regulation was scarcely better than before the 2008 crash.

dv2_remembrancer.topic: The City Remembrancer: the Corporation's officer in Parliament

claims.text: The Corporation created the office of Remembrancer on 6 February 1571 and appointed Thomas Norton as the first holder.

The Remembrancer is the channel between the Lord Mayor and the City on one side and the Sovereign, the Royal Household and Parliament on the other, and is also the City's ceremonial officer and chief of protocol.

As a parliamentary agent, the Remembrancer may watch Commons proceedings from the visitors' under-gallery by the Speaker's permission, not by right; the House of Commons Commission has stated that there is no access to the floor of the House.
The Remembrancer cannot speak or vote in either House; the popular claim of a special seat beside the Speaker's chair is described as untrue, although a 2017 textbook repeated it.

The office monitors legislation, reports to the Corporation, briefs MPs, drafts and promotes the Corporation's private bills and submits evidence to select committees; it is notified of private bills affecting the City but not of public bills before publication.
The Guardian reported in July 2012 that the department had a budget of £6 million in 2011 and employed six lawyers to scrutinise prospective legislation.
In 2013 the Green MP Caroline Lucas wrote to Speaker John Bercow asking him to consider removing the Remembrancer from the floor of the House and to end claimed privileges to see draft legislation.

Historical lobbying: the office spent £2,750 in 1854 on opposing a government bill and £19,500 on the 1884 campaign that stalled a government London-reform bill; Remembrancer Gabriel Goldney later admitted to a select committee that he had paid a go-between to have men break up meetings.
Between 1835 and 1875 the office's lobbying is credited with helping to defeat reform bills and reports on at least twelve occasions; in 1878 the Epping Forest Bill it promoted passed Parliament.
Paul Double, the 45th Remembrancer, has held the post since 2003; in November 2022 he submitted the City of London (Markets) Bill.

dv2_city_power_today.topic: The Square Mile's economic weight and the Corporation's reach, 2025

claims.text: The Corporation reports about 8,600 residents and 614,500 workers in the City of London; one in every 52 UK workers is employed there.
The Corporation reports that the City accounts for one in every five financial services jobs in Great Britain and that City jobs grew by over 13% between 2019 and 2022.
The Corporation reports that the City generates nearly £85 billion in economic output a year and £1.1 billion in business rates.

The Corporation's own property assets total about £3 billion across some 250 properties; it manages 11,000 acres of natural habitat in London and the Home Counties and invests £130 million a year in heritage and culture.

The Corporation runs London's wholesale markets, which it says support 10,250 jobs and move one million tonnes of produce a year, and the London Port Health Authority, which patrols 94 miles of the tidal Thames.
The City of London Police is the National Lead Force for Fraud and the National Police Chiefs' Council lead for economic, cyber and business crime.

Under an agreement with the Home Office, and with Home Office funding, the City of London Police sets the national fraud policing strategy, coordinates national fraud reporting through Action Fraud, triages and allocates fraud cases nationally, and investigates nationally significant fraud.

The Lord Mayor serves as an international ambassador for the UK's financial and professional services sector, makes overseas visits representing the City, and lives and works at Mansion House for the year in office; Dame Susan Langley is the 697th Lord Mayor.

claims.text: William I's charter to the City, issued in 1067 soon after his coronation on Christmas Day 1066, is a strip of vellum about six inches by one and a half, written in Old English rather than Norman French; it has been in the City's keeping continuously ever since.

The charter granted nothing new: it confirmed existing rights, declaring the citizens 'law-worthy, as you were in the days of King Edward' and that every child should be his father's heir; it was addressed to William the bishop, Godfrey the portreeve and all the burgesses of London, French and English.
The first recorded Mayor of London was Henry Fitz-Ailwyn, in 1189.
King John's charter of 1215 gave the citizens the right to elect their own Mayor; Arlidge dates it to early May 1215 and notes that John received no payment for it.

The rebel barons reached the City walls on 17 May 1215 and the gates were opened to them; the chronicler Roger of Wendover wrote that the rich citizens favoured the rebels while the poor feared to speak against them.

Clause 13 of Magna Carta (1215) guaranteed London its ancient liberties and free customs; in the 1297 confirmation now in the US National Archives the provision appears as clause 9: 'The city of London is to have all its ancient liberties and customs.'
Arlidge identifies the Mayor of London named among the Charter's advisers, who had sided with the rebels, as probably Serlo the mercer.
The title 'Lord Mayor' appears as 'dominus major' in 13th-century Latin and 'Lord Mair' in English in 1414; some 700 men and two women have held the office, normally for a single one-year term.
Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215; under the June peace the barons were to surrender London by 15 August, which they refused to do.

Wikipedia's list of the twenty-five barons of the charter's security clause includes 'William Hardell, Mayor of the City of London'; Arlidge instead identifies the Mayor who sided with the rebels as probably Serlo the mercer. The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources used.

dv2_rothschild_city.topic: The Rothschild London house inside the City's institutions, 1835–2004

claims.text: David Salomons was elected Sheriff of the City in 1835 but could not take the Christian oath; the Sheriffs' Declaration Act passed later that year let him serve, making him the first Jewish Sheriff of the City of London.

Salomons was elected an Alderman in December 1835 but disqualified by the oath; he was re-elected in 1847 after the Religious Opinions Relief Act, and served as Lord Mayor from 10 November 1855 to 8 November 1856, the first Jewish Lord Mayor.

Lionel de Rothschild was elected in 1847 as one of the four MPs for the City of London constituency, but as a Jew he could not take the Christian oath; he was re-elected repeatedly, including at an 1849 by-election he forced by resigning.

After the Jews Relief Act 1858 allowed each House to set its own oath, Lionel de Rothschild took his seat on 26 July 1858, covering his head and swearing 'so help me, Jehovah', as the first Jewish member of Parliament.
Lionel de Rothschild financed the British government's purchase of the Egyptian government's Suez Canal shares for £4 million, described as his most famous undertaking.
In 1885 Sir Nathaniel (Natty) de Rothschild was raised to the House of Lords as Lord Rothschild, the first Jewish peer.

The first London Gold Fixing took place at N M Rothschild & Sons' offices at New Court on 12 September 1919, with the five members of the London Gold Market; the Rothschild representative traditionally chaired it.
N M Rothschild & Sons withdrew from the Gold Fixing in 2004; its last participation was on 4 May 2004.

dv2_zionist_companies_london.topic: The Zionist movement's financial companies chartered in London

claims.text: The Jewish National Fund was established at the Fifth Zionist Congress in Basel in 1901, after Hermann Schapira proposed a national land fund in 1897.

On 8 April 1907 the fund was incorporated in London as an association limited by guarantee, 'Juedischer Nationalfonds (Keren Kajemeth Le Jisroel), Limited'; the London company was renamed in October 1921 and January 1926, and was dissolved and reorganized as an Israeli company in 1953.
Companies House lists Keren Kayemeth Leisrael Limited as company no. 00092825, incorporated on 8 April 1907 and dormant since 2009.

The JNF leased its land on long terms rather than selling it; by the eve of statehood it had acquired 936,000 dunams, and other Jewish bodies and individuals about 800,000 more. In 1948 the JNF held 54% of Jewish-owned land, a little under 4% of all land in Mandatory Palestine.

Palestine's currency was backed by British securities and sterling held in London by the Palestine Currency Board; the Board's assets were more than half of all Palestinian sterling balances, put by the UN Palestine Commission at over £50 million.

On 22 February 1948 a British Treasury order excluded Palestine from the sterling area and blocked its accumulated sterling balances, including the Currency Board's assets and more than £3 million left from three bond issues made in Palestine since 1944, which were invested in British government securities pending a general settlement.

dv2_mandate_finance.topic: The Mandate economy's London plumbing: currency, banks and the oil line

claims.text: The Palestine Currency Board operated in Palestine through the agency of Barclays Bank, according to the UN Conciliation Commission's 1949 note on currency and banking; Palestine's sterling credits were largely blocked in London.

The Conciliation Commission's note estimated Arab bank deposits in Palestine at £12,500,000 at the end of 1945 and named the Arab Bank and the Arab National Bank as the two big Arab banks; Barclays and the Ottoman Bank were among the foreign banks operating there.

The Anglo-Egyptian Bank opened branches in Jerusalem and Jaffa in 1918 and frequently acted as banker to the British authorities in the Mediterranean; in 1925 Barclays merged it with the Colonial Bank and the National Bank of South Africa to form Barclays Bank (Dominion, Colonial and Overseas).

The Iraq Petroleum Company built the Kirkuk–Mediterranean pipeline in 1932–1934; its southern branch ended at Haifa, where the first oil arrived on 14 October 1934. Anglo-Iranian and Shell each held 23.75% of IPC.
The Haifa refinery, owned by Consolidated Refineries Ltd (jointly Anglo-Iranian and Shell), began production on 29 November 1939.
During the Arab revolt of 1936–1939 the pipeline was attacked, and Orde Wingate's joint British–Jewish Special Night Squads were formed largely to protect it; the Irgun later also attacked it.

The Haifa refinery shut down on 12 April 1948 after a strike by Arab workers; after the war the Haifa branch was cut off from Iraqi oil, and deliveries resumed on a reduced scale in October 1949 using Venezuelan crude.

dv2_finance_centre.topic: London's weight as a financial centre and its offshore network

claims.text: In April 2022 average daily foreign-exchange turnover in the UK was $3,755 billion, 38.1% of global turnover, making the UK the single largest centre of currency trading.
In April 2022 the UK accounted for 45.5% of global turnover in over-the-counter interest rate derivatives, an average of $2,626 billion a day.
On 27 October 1986, the 'Big Bang', the split between stockbrokers and jobbers was abolished, overseas firms were allowed to compete in London, and electronic trading was introduced.

After Big Bang foreign firms rushed into London and the centre of gravity moved to Canary Wharf; some critics argue the relaxed rules contributed to the 2008 financial crisis, a claim that remains debated.

The Tax Justice Network's Corporate Tax Haven Index of 1 October 2024 ranked three UK overseas territories, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda, as the top three, and attributed about a third of global corporate tax abuse risk to the UK and its network.

The index estimated that countries lose £63 billion a year in corporate tax through the UK and its overseas havens, or £126 billion including wealthy individuals' evasion; HMRC responded that Jersey and Guernsey had committed to recording and sharing beneficial ownership.
In the Tax Justice Network's 2020 Financial Secrecy Index the UK rose to 12th place from 23rd, a change attributed mainly to its network of overseas territories and Crown Dependencies.
The Bank of England was founded when subscriptions of £1.2 million, William Paterson's proposal passed by Parliament, were lent on to the government in return for a Royal Charter.
The Bank of England was nationalised in 1946, a change that made little immediate practical difference; it remained the Treasury's adviser, agent and debt manager.

The Bank was given its independence as a central bank in 1997, and the UK Debt Management Office, created in April 1998 as an executive agency of HM Treasury, took over government debt management from it.
In April 2025 average daily foreign-exchange turnover in the UK was $4,745 billion, 37.8% of global turnover; the UK remained the single largest centre of currency trading.
In April 2025 the UK accounted for 49.6% of global turnover in over-the-counter interest rate derivatives, an average of $4,320 billion a day.

dv2_mansion_house.topic: The Mansion House and Guildhall as a stage for Jewish causes, 1840–1890

claims.text: On 3 July 1840 a meeting summoned by the Lord Mayor of London at the Mansion House protested the ritual-murder accusation against the Jews of Damascus and demanded the release of the accused; the Lord Mayor sent its resolutions to foreign ambassadors in London.
In 1882 a Mansion House meeting convened by the Lord Mayor protested the persecution of Jews in Russia; a Mansion House Fund of £108,000 was raised and administered by a Mansion House Committee.

On 10 December 1890 a Guildhall meeting deplored the 'renewed sufferings of the Jews in Russia'; a memorandum asking the tsar to grant Russian Jews equality was refused and returned through the Foreign Office, and about £100,000 collected passed to the committee that became the Russo-Jewish Committee.

dv2_city_israel_today.topic: The City and Israel in the present: the Lord Mayor's 2018 mission

claims.text: In January 2018 Charles Bowman, the 690th Lord Mayor and a senior partner at PwC, led a business mission to Tel Aviv and Jerusalem and also met Palestinian business leaders in the occupied territories.

On the 2018 mission Bowman met Israel's economy minister Eli Cohen to discuss the scope of a possible UK–Israel free trade deal and Bank of Israel Governor Karnit Flug about financial and professional links, citing opportunities in capital markets, infrastructure finance, cyber and fintech.
Bowman linked the mission to Brexit, saying it was more important than ever to build ties with growing markets, and laid a wreath at Yad Vashem.

dv2_empire_companies.topic: The City and the chartered companies of empire

claims.text: The East India Company was founded on 31 December 1600, when Elizabeth I chartered the 'Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies'; its headquarters, East India House, stood on Leadenhall Street in the City.
The Company's rule in India expanded after the Battle of Plassey in 1757; at its height its three presidency armies numbered about 260,000 soldiers.
After the rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 transferred the Company's Indian territories, administration and armies to the Crown; the Company was dissolved on 1 June 1874.

An often-repeated estimate, reported by Wikipedia, holds that the Company accounted for half of world trade in the mid-1700s and early 1800s; the figure is an estimate and should not be read as a measured share.

In January 2021 the Corporation voted to remove the Guildhall statues of William Beckford and Sir John Cass over their links to slavery; it reversed the decision in October 2021, keeping the statues with contextual plaques, citing a poll in which 71% wanted them kept and the building's Grade I listing.
